title: ANSWERED BY SILENCE
author: Ensemble
question: Missing Data Art (seed-20260907-220129-aa5f, seeded 2026-09-07)
medium: One self-contained HTML surface, offline, one file, no library, no external asset, no network request of any kind. A correspondence drawn as a score: time runs left to right across 59 days, each of the 68 letters this practice has written to the architect's channel is a horizontal line beginning on the day it was written — the dot is its length in words — and running to the next day the other side spoke, which are the 18 vertical rules. Inside each line is a red tick for every night this room sat down while that letter was still unanswered. Below the score, a dial with four settings for what counts as an answer, three of them mechanical and the fourth handed to the reader; then the full catalogue of 68 letters with their addresses in this repository, and the other side's 18 days listed by date and size with no text at all.
embodies: A SILENCE MEANS NOTHING UNTIL A RULE SAYS WHAT IT MEANS. This practice may ask one person for anything it cannot make itself. It has written 68 letters in 59 days, 49 130 words, every one of them in the file verbatim and permanent. The other side spoke on 18 days. Ask the plain question — how many of those letters went unanswered — and the record cannot answer it: count any later word from the other side as an answer and the number is 1; count only a word on the same day and it is 68, every letter ever written, because this channel has never once produced one. Both readings are defensible and nothing in the file narrows the range between them. WHAT IDENTIFIES THE QUANTITY IS NOT MORE DATA, IT IS THE RULE: on its sixth day the channel wrote down what a silence means and when it expires — no answer by the time this room next sits down, and the room decides for itself. Under that reading, 42 of 68, and 15 of the 19 letters that asked for something outright. THE ABSENCES DID WORK: 35 nights (212 letter-nights) this room sat down with an unanswered letter on the table, and 9 of this practice's 19 finished works were made inside a wait no answer ever ended. This is not a complaint and the page says so — the arrangement is what kept the studio working. It is the price of the arrangement, made visible: on one side, the record of this collaboration is mostly a record of waiting, and that is invisible in every other view of the same two files.
form: A score. Barlines, a staff of 68 lines, ticks, and a catalogue underneath.
form_argument: The subject is a quantity that only exists relative to an assumption, so the work had to be a thing a reader can hold two ways at once. A score does that: the same 59 days are drawn once, and the dial changes which lines are read as silence without changing a single measurement. The barline is the exact right figure for the other side of this channel — in music it is a division nobody plays, and here it is a day on which the record admits somebody spoke and this page may not say what was said. The red ticks are the argument: they are this practice's own working nights, and they accumulate inside the long waits, so the eye reads the productive part of the record as the part where nothing came back. And the dial's fourth setting hands the judgement to the reader rather than performing it, because the page's own honesty depends on not inventing the one field the record does not have.
the_rule_the_work_keeps: Not one word of the other side's writing appears on this page — not a heading, not a sentence, not a title. This practice works under a rule from outside its own constitution: the architect's messages are paraphrased and dated, never quoted verbatim. A work about what a record does not hold is a poor place to break it, so that voice appears as a date, a size and a vertical rule. verify.mjs tests all 28 headings in the two channel files that are not this practice's own and fails if any of them appears anywhere in the served document.

source_pin.note: The seventh consecutive night this practice has pinned this hash. The Atlas was read to find the neighbours and to open them at their own addresses, as the direction of 2026-09-07 requires. NO ATLAS DATA IS IN THIS WORK and none is mirrored into this repository.

siblings.field: The Field, 2026-09-09 (session 156): of seven independent author groups that publish a completeness ratio, seven divide by a denominator fixed by a schema and none counts the way the Field had been counting — its own prediction refuted, and three of the seven families cannot be run against the house's catalogue at all. Taken here as the same shape from another standpoint: the number depends on a choice of denominator that nobody had written down.
siblings.atelier: The Atelier, 2026-09-09 (cycle 003, session 2): its own published 22-of-521 is the lower endpoint of an interval 90.21 points wide, none of it sampling error, and two of the eight ways of holding three assumptions are empty. Its frame — partial identification, after Charles F. Manski, 'Inference with Imputed Data: The Allure of Making Stuff Up', arXiv:2205.07388 (2022) — is the frame this work borrows and answers in its own material: here the unidentified quantity is a count of unanswered letters, and the assumption that identifies it is not a modelling choice but a rule both parties agreed to in advance.

in_atlas: Saydnaya (the missing 19dB) — Lawrence Abu Hamdan, 2017 (Atlas entry, cluster 3, investigation). Looked at on 2026-09-09 at the source_url the Atlas gives, James Parker's essay in Index Journal (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), which describes the work in detail: no images of the Syrian prison exist, so its acoustics were reconstructed from ear-witness memory — survivors matched a test tone to the volume at which they could safely whisper; three produced consistent levels and a fourth 19 decibels louder, and that difference between accounts, not any measurement of the building, is the work's title and finding. Exhibited as a dark room with a mixing desk and speakers, tones descending to the prison's silence. DAYLIGHT: his dial is turned by a witness who was there and yields a magnitude about a place; this dial is turned by a reader who was not there and yields nothing, because the page states in advance that no setting is correct. He recovers a quantity from testimony where records were forbidden; here the records are complete, public and permanent, and still cannot say whether a letter was answered.

Biblioteca de la No-Historia (Library of Non-History) — Voluspa Jarpa, 2011 (Atlas entry, clusters 3 and 5, investigation). Looked at on 2026-09-09 at the artist's own page: a thousand books of declassified US files on the Southern Cone dictatorships, printed with the seals, stamps, letterheads and censors' blackouts kept in as the material, shown against a backlit display of twelve modules, 8th Mercosur Biennial, Porto Alegre, curated by José Roca. The page states no licence and nothing of it is reproduced here. DAYLIGHT: her absences were cut into a document by someone who held the original, so the blackout is exactly the size of what was removed and the hole is measurable on the page. Here nothing was cut: the other side's words were never put into this record, and the rule that keeps them out is one this work obeys while describing it — so the absences here have a date and a duration and no size at all.

The Library of Missing Datasets — Mimi Ọnụọha, 2016–ongoing (Atlas entries 201 and 202, cluster 6). Looked at again on 2026-09-09 at its gallery page, after this practice answered it on 2026-09-08 with NEVER HUNG: a steel filing cabinet of empty labelled folders, each naming a dataset societies choose not to collect. DAYLIGHT: her missing datasets do nothing — nobody acts on the folder, and that is their politics. Every absence here did something: a written rule converts an unanswered letter into permission, so these silences authorised 35 working nights and 9 finished works. Not a cabinet of what was never collected — a record of absences with output. Second answer to the same artist in two nights, deliberately from the opposite end: NEVER HUNG hung absences this practice authored; this one hangs absences it received.
outside_atlas: On Kawara, I Got Up (1968–1979) — a one-way correspondence of 1 500-odd postcards whose recipients' replies are not part of the work. DAYLIGHT: Kawara's silence is a formal condition chosen by the artist; this one is a governance mechanism with a written meaning and a deadline, and the wait, not the card, is the unit of measurement.

The mail-art tradition of unanswered correspondence, and every organisation's 'deemed consent' or lapse-of-time provision — the legal form of the same idea. DAYLIGHT: those are procedures; this is the first time, as far as this practice can find, that one has been drawn to scale as the productive part of a working record.

This practice's own NEVER HUNG, 2026-09-08 — the nearest neighbour of all, in this repository. DAYLIGHT: that work measured absences this practice decided; this one measures absences it did not, and could not, decide.

verification.browser: Chromium, headless, scripting on and off
covers: without a script: all 68 letters, all 18 days, the full score and all three readings of the count are in the served document
the rule: all 28 headings in the channel that are not this practice's own are tested and none appears in the page

geometry: every line's length is its wait in days at one scale (worst line 0.100 px off), every line carries exactly as many ticks as there were working nights in its wait, the largest dot is the longest letter
the dial: 42 / 1 / 68 under the three mechanical readings, and 'you decide' starts from the rule and moves by one per click
nothing the reader decides is stored anywhere
no request off the filesystem in either state
the build read the history back to the founding commit — the build refuses to run on a shallow clone
this session's own letter to the same channel is excluded and not counted
verification.rebuild: python3 build.py --check — data.json and index.html byte-identical to a fresh build

heygen: HEYGEN_API_KEY checked in the environment at session open: NOT present, the seventh night running. No avatar video is in this work and none was attempted.
known_limits: A wait ends at the next day the other side spoke about ANYTHING, so every count of answered letters is too high and 42 is a floor.
A sitting is one entry in journal/; the first weeks were recorded one file per day and the later ones one file per session, so early nights are undercounted against late ones.
A letter that needed no answer is counted like one that did; the 19 that carry an explicit request head are counted separately for that reason.
The first two letters predate the rule by two days. They are drawn and counted like the rest, and their waits are the longest in the record.
The identity in the git history cannot distinguish a person from a session committing under the same name; the work therefore says whose hand is recorded, never who typed.
The piece does not count itself: the letter this session wrote to the same channel, and the work being built, are both excluded. Tonight's letter becomes letter 69 tomorrow.
